headline: Burnt Coconut Bait Leads to Discovery of New Mouse Species in Sri Lanka
meta_description: Scientists formally described Mus dumbara, a spiny mouse endemic to Sri Lanka's Knuckles Mountain Range, after 20 years of analysis following its 2004 discover…
summary_short: A new species of spiny mouse from Sri Lanka's Knuckles Mountains was formally described after two decades of study—and it was burnt coconut that helped catch it.
body:
In March 2004, researchers working the forest edge near Puwakpitiya village made an unexpected discovery: two tiny mice, no larger than a child's palm, caught in traps baited with burnt coconut. The bait choice proved crucial—peanut butter, the standard rodent lure, had failed to attract Sri Lankan mice. Those two specimens, both females with fulvous-gray fur and unusually long tails, looked different from known species, but their true significance remained hidden for over two decades. Only after careful morphological and genetic analysis—which revealed more than 11.7% genetic divergence from related species—did scientists formally confirm what they had long suspected: a species entirely new to science. The mouse was named Mus dumbara, linking it to the Dumbara valley within the Knuckles Mountain Range where it was found.

What makes this discovery remarkable is how elusive the creature has proven since. Despite investing 1,900 trap nights in 2014 and 2015 using identical methods, researchers failed to capture another specimen, leaving fundamental questions about the mouse's current population and true range unanswered. The species has been recorded only from one valley in the UNESCO World Heritage Site, though it may inhabit other unsurveyed forest fragments or exist at extremely low densities.

The find underscores a deeper truth about Sri Lanka's biodiversity. The island, which forms part of one of the world's most recognized biodiversity hotspots alongside India's Western Ghats, harbors exceptional endemism in its wet-zone and montane forests. Yet smaller mammals have been far less studied than frogs, lizards, and crabs. With habitat pressures—road construction, land clearance, plantation expansion—already threatening forest margins even within protected areas, the discovery of Mus dumbara highlights both the island's overlooked richness and the urgent need for broader surveys to understand what else remains unknown.
quick_facts: Two female mice caught in March 2004 at Puwakpitiya village, Knuckles Range
Took 20+ years of genetic and morphological analysis to confirm new species
Burnt coconut used as bait instead of unsuccessful peanut butter lure
1,900 trap nights in 2014-2015 failed to find additional specimens
Sri Lanka now home to seven endemic rat and mouse species
